title: Chapter 5 — Cause and Effect
paragraphs: Gaew lays out the town's physics: tham dii dai dii, tham chua dai chua — do good, meet good; do bad, meet bad. Karma in Mae Jaeng is not fatalism but moral causation running on intention, and the chapter maps its everyday uses: the tsunami, a motorbike accident ("that's my karma"), Mae Daeng reading her widowhood through merit, P'Dao weighing the late police chief's fortune.

Its finer points get argued around the fire. Can merit cancel bad karma? A visiting Bangkok monk offers the salt-in-water image — the salt remains, but diluted. Mae Daeng and her sister Mae Lah say yes; Niw, visiting from America, will only give it "fifty-fifty." Goy, the town's deepest reader, offers the subtlest account: karmas "talk to each other" (khui gan), and merit made expecting a reward is barely merit at all. Intention — cetana — is everything.

Then theory meets Sen. Julia returns from Chicago to find him skeletal and yellow, the shop no longer selling alcohol, the saint-monk Khruba Si Wichai's portrait where the whiskey used to be — and a kitchen knife above Sen's bed against any rescue. Twelve-year-old Noi, it turns out, has been passing whiskey through the window daily; kindness, in a boy's understanding.

The first ambulance attempt fails: Ban breaks down the door, Sen brandishes the knife, and his friends — cool-hearted to the last — back away. While he sleeps, Julia slips the knife into her pocket. It is the ethnography's most argued-over moment: the observer intervening, one culture's model of agency overriding another's. Five policemen carry Sen out on a stretcher; Chai arranges the ambulance and lifts his friend in his arms — the one act, of the whole rescue, that Sen will later say he remembers.

The hospitals do what they can, which is little: Suan Prung turns him away as "too far gone"; Nakhon Ping diagnoses cirrhosis and two hepatitis strains in a two-hundred-bed ward; the private Chiang Mai Ram adds a feeding tube while Sen ashes imaginary cigarettes. His parents arrive late — they had merit-making to finish first, for his sake, because merit is the medicine they can administer. Only Dee, from England, says aloud that the calm is madness. A frank nurse repeats the Prologue's instruction: tham jai, take him home.

Home, unconscious, on his and Noi's shared birthday, Sen receives every treatment the valley has: Nan Jon's khwan rite detaching the spirits of alcohol, the whole family's merit, and — down from Ban Ko Tao — Jerapong's congregation praying over a Buddhist's bed. Moh Bom closes the loop with the word he began with: anicca. Past midnight, Gaew makes her confession and her decision — close the shop, stop selling what killed him, live a peaceful life.
